What is SuperUnicode?

The character system, the machine instructions and the storage framing of the OpenWindows kernel.

SuperUnicode is the native character encoding of the OpenWindows kernel. When OpenWindows reads a string, names a file or lays out a data file, it assumes SuperUnicode — no encoding negotiation, no code pages, no transcoding.

What it contains

  • A character system. Codepoints in a 31-bit space, organized into a fixed hierarchy.
  • A Unicode bridge. The low range is permanently 1:1 with Unicode.
  • Machine instructions. Codepoints can be instructions that the kernel executes, not just glyphs.
  • A database. Every codepoint, block, property, name and mapping is machine-readable (SUCD).
  • Storage and transport. Framing (SUTF), serialization (SUST), storage (OWFS/USFS) and extended transport (vsutf/e-SUST).

Why “native”?

An encoding is native when the system’s lowest layers assume it. In OpenWindows the kernel itself reads and emits SuperUnicode streams: the compiler, the filesystem, the diagnostics and the boot loader all speak the same encoding, so nothing is ever reinterpreted.
